381: B is correct because Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is PostgreSQL-compatible, so the existing relational queries and application code require the least change. An Aurora Replica lets the monthly reporting queries run against the reader endpoint, which isolates the long-running workload from the primary instance so document modifications and new inserts continue without contention. Aurora also scales read capacity easily while sharing the same storage volume as the primary for low lag.
382: A is correct because configuring a TLS listener on the Network Load Balancer encrypts the sensor data in transit between the users' devices and the load balancer, and deploying the server certificate on the NLB enables native TLS termination. This protects data in motion at the edge of the three-tier flow without changing the architecture. The other options address DDoS protection or encryption at rest rather than encryption in transit.
383: A is correct because socket- and core-based licensing is tied to physical hardware, and Dedicated Hosts provide the dedicated physical server capacity required to reuse the company's existing licenses. Reserved pricing for the Dedicated Host offers a substantial discount over On-Demand for workloads with predictable capacity and uptime requirements, making it the most cost-effective option. Reserved or On-Demand Instances do not guarantee control over physical placement, which this licensing model requires.
384: C is correct because Amazon EFS is a POSIX-compliant shared file system that can be mounted concurrently across all the EC2 instances and Availability Zones. The EFS Standard storage class stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones, providing the high availability and maximum durability required. The lifecycle management policy that transitions data to EFS Standard-IA after the first 30 days reduces storage costs for the infrequently accessed data while keeping it in the same shared file system, whereas S3 is not POSIX-compliant and EFS One Zone lacks multi-AZ durability.
385: C is correct because security groups are stateful and can reference other security groups as the traffic source, enabling least-privilege chaining. Allowing port 443 on the web servers only from the load balancer prevents direct internet access to the web tier, and allowing port 3306 on MySQL only from the web servers' security group restricts database access to the application tier alone. This chained configuration gives each resource only the access it needs, satisfying the company policy.
386: B is correct because Amazon ElastiCache provides an in-memory caching layer that stores the frequently requested identical datasets. Serving these repeated reads from cache removes the redundant database calls that are causing the backend performance slowdowns, reducing load on the RDS for MySQL instance. A read replica scales reads but does not cache identical result sets the way ElastiCache does.
387: D is correct because creating a new IAM user for the deployment engineer and placing the user in a group whose policy allows only AWS CloudFormation actions ensures the engineer can perform stack operations with no unnecessary permissions, following the principle of least privilege. E is correct because creating an IAM role that explicitly defines the permissions specific to the stack and launching the stack with that role scopes exactly what the deployment can create and manage. Together these actions avoid the excessive rights of PowerUsers or AdministratorAccess and never require root user credentials.
388: D is correct because a security group denies all inbound traffic by default, so the RDS instance's security group must have an explicit rule allowing port 3306 from the web tier's security group before the application can connect. Network ACLs in their default state already allow all traffic, and routing between subnets in the same VPC is automatic, so the missing security group rule is the cause of the connection failure.
389: A is correct because RDS read replicas provide a dedicated read-only endpoint for the business reporting queries, isolating the heavy read workload from the production DB instance. This allows reporting to run without affecting write operations on the source database. A Multi-AZ deployment improves availability but the standby does not serve read traffic.
390: A is correct because sticky sessions (session affinity) on the ALB keep each customer's requests on the same backend instance during a transaction, providing consistent session handling as the application scales. D is correct because Amazon ElastiCache for Redis is a fast, persistent store for customer session information that lives outside the EC2 instances, so session data survives instance termination or replacement and satisfies the durability requirement. Together these options optimize session management without rebuilding the application's session logic.
391: C is correct because the web application is stateless with no temporary local storage, so retaining the latest AMIs of the web and application tiers is sufficient to rebuild the fleet and works seamlessly with Auto Scaling, maximizing scalability. Enabling automated backups on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL provides point-in-time recovery that easily meets the 2-hour RPO for the database tier. This avoids wasteful frequent EBS snapshots of stateless instances and optimizes resource utilization.
392: A is correct because customers have dynamic IP addresses, so the web servers' security group must allow inbound HTTPS on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 for global accessibility. The DB instance's security group should allow inbound port 3306 only from the web servers' security group so the database is never reachable from the internet. Referencing security groups keeps the database tier protected even as customer IP addresses change.
393: C is correct because Amazon Transcribe is the AWS service that converts audio recordings to text and natively supports PII redaction. Turning on PII redaction in the transcription job automatically removes personally identifiable information from the transcript, and an S3 upload event can invoke a Lambda function to start the job and store the redacted output in a separate bucket. Textract analyzes images and documents rather than audio files.
394: C is correct because Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes are designed for I/O-intensive, latency-sensitive database workloads and can deliver the sustained performance needed above the 20,000 IOPS threshold where the application degrades. A gp3 volume cannot be provisioned beyond 16,000 IOPS, so it cannot meet the observed high-demand requirement. Splitting into two smaller gp3 volumes does not help because the database needs a single high-performance volume.
395: C is correct because AWS CloudTrail records the API calls made in the account, including the identity of the IAM user, the time of each call, and which resources were changed, such as security group modifications. Reviewing the CloudTrail event history from the production deployment reveals exactly which IAM user made the undesired security group changes. GuardDuty and Inspector detect threats and vulnerabilities rather than attributing configuration changes to specific users.
396: A is correct because AWS Shield Advanced provides managed DDoS protection and explicitly supports AWS Global Accelerator as a protected resource type. Adding the accelerator as a protected resource shields the entire solution at its entry point, since all client traffic flows through the accelerator endpoints, and Global Accelerator's static anycast IPs further absorb volumetric floods. Shield Advanced also includes 24/7 DDoS response team support and cost protection.
397: C is correct because the job can run up to an hour, which exceeds the 15-minute maximum execution time of AWS Lambda. An ECS cluster with the Fargate launch type runs the containerized job serverlessly, matching the known CPU and memory requirements with no EC2 instances to patch, provision, or manage. An EventBridge scheduled event launches the Fargate task once a day, minimizing operational effort.
398: C is correct because transferring 600 TB over a 100 Mbps connection would take far longer than the required 2 weeks, so any network-based transfer is not feasible. AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices can move the full dataset offline within the window, and the data is encrypted on the device and in transit with KMS-managed keys, meeting the sensitivity requirement. This one-time bulk transfer is also more cost-effective than provisioning a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link.
399: B is correct because an AWS WAF rate-based rule automatically blocks requests originating from a single source IP once the request count exceeds a defined threshold within a 5-minute window, which directly mitigates HTTP flood attacks. Associating the Regional web ACL with the API Gateway stage applies the protection exactly where requests arrive with no infrastructure to manage. This has far less operational overhead than building a custom Lambda@Edge blocking solution or relying on manual CloudWatch alarms.
400: C is correct because Amazon DynamoDB Streams captures every new item written to the table without any change to the existing application's write path, so the current application's performance is unaffected. A trigger processes the stream record and publishes to a single SNS topic, and each of the four teams simply subscribes to that topic with its preferred protocol. This fully managed, event-driven approach delivers the alerts with the least operational overhead.
